name: Fibula
func: The thin outer bone of the lower leg. It carries little weight but anchors many muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle joint, keeping the ankle stable.

levels.kid:
Next to your big shinbone is a skinny bone called the **fibula**. It is on the outside of your leg, near your little toe side.

It does not hold up much of your weight. Instead, it is like a **helper**. Lots of leg muscles hold onto it, and at the bottom it makes the **bump on the outside of your ankle**. That bump helps keep your ankle from wobbling and twisting.

The fibula is so thin and bendy that doctors can sometimes borrow a piece of it to fix other bones in the body!
levels.hs:
The **fibula** is the long, slender bone on the **lateral** (outer) side of the leg, running parallel to the tibia. Its name means "brooch pin" in Latin, because next to the tibia it looks like the pin of a clasp.

At the top, its **head** sits just below and behind the outer knee, joined to the underside of the tibia's lateral condyle at the **proximal tibiofibular joint**. It does not take part in the knee joint itself. The **lateral collateral ligament** of the knee and the **biceps femoris** tendon attach to the head.

At the bottom, it ends as the **lateral malleolus**, the bony bump on the outside of the ankle. This reaches lower than the medial malleolus and grips the outer side of the talus, forming the **ankle mortise** with the tibia.

The fibula carries only a small share of body weight (commonly quoted as around 10–15%). Its main jobs are to give attachment to muscles, mainly the **fibular (peroneal)** muscles and deep calf muscles, and to stabilise the ankle. It is joined to the tibia along its length by the **interosseous membrane**.
levels.college:
The fibula has a head, neck, shaft and distal lateral malleolus. Its shaft is twisted and has several borders and surfaces that separate muscle groups: the **lateral compartment** (fibularis longus and brevis), the **anterior compartment** (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the **posterior compartment** (soleus superficially, tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus deeply).

**Key relation:** the **common fibular nerve** winds around the **fibular neck**, directly against bone and just under the skin, before dividing into the **superficial fibular nerve** (to the lateral compartment and skin of the dorsum of the foot) and the **deep fibular nerve** (to the anterior compartment and the first web space).

**Joints:** the proximal tibiofibular joint is a plane synovial joint that allows slight gliding. Distally, the **tibiofibular syndesmosis** is a fibrous joint held by the anterior and posterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments and the interosseous ligament. During ankle dorsiflexion the wider front of the talus wedges into the mortise, and the fibula moves slightly outward and rotates to accommodate it.

**Lateral ankle ligaments** arise from the lateral malleolus: the **anterior talofibular (ATFL)**, **calcaneofibular (CFL)** and **posterior talofibular** ligaments. The fibularis longus and brevis tendons pass in a groove behind the malleolus under the superior fibular retinaculum.

Nutrient supply comes from the **fibular (peroneal) artery**, a branch of the posterior tibial artery, which runs close to the bone's posterior surface.
levels.phd:
Although classed as a minor weight-bearer, the fibula's load share is debated: cadaver and finite-element studies report figures from about 6% to over 15% of axial load depending on ankle position and loading, and it may carry more during dorsiflexion and single-leg stance. Its main mechanical role is probably to stabilise the mortise and act as a lateral buttress.

Embryologically, the fibula arises from the postaxial (lateral) side of the limb bud mesenchyme. Its development depends on posterior limb patterning signals, including **Sonic hedgehog** from the zone of polarizing activity. **Fibular hemimelia**, a congenital partial or complete absence of the fibula, is the most common congenital long-bone deficiency and is usually accompanied by a short tibia, ankle instability and missing lateral rays of the foot, underscoring the shared patterning field.

The fibula's anatomy makes it the workhorse of **vascularised bone transfer**. The **fibular artery** supplies the diaphysis through a nutrient artery and a series of periosteal branches, and gives **septocutaneous perforators** through the posterior crural septum to overlying skin. The middle segment can be harvested with its vessels as a **free fibula flap**, leaving roughly 6 cm proximally (to protect the common fibular nerve and knee stability) and 6 cm distally (to preserve the ankle mortise). Because it has a straight, dense cortex, it can be cut into segments and shaped to rebuild the jaw after tumour resection. Donor-site function is usually well preserved, which supports the view that the bone is not essential for gait in most people.
levels.expert:
**Ankle fractures** most commonly involve the lateral malleolus. The **Weber classification** grades them by fracture height relative to the syndesmosis: **Weber A** below it (usually stable), **Weber B** at the level of it (variable), and **Weber C** above it (syndesmosis disrupted, usually unstable and fixed surgically). Stability depends on the **deltoid ligament** medially too; a widened medial clear space on a stress X-ray suggests instability.

The **Ottawa ankle rules** guide X-ray: bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps.

A **Maisonneuve fracture** is a high proximal fibular fracture combined with a syndesmotic and medial ankle injury; always palpate the whole fibula in an ankle injury. A **high ankle sprain** (syndesmotic injury) is tested with the **squeeze test** and external rotation stress.

The most common ankle sprain tears the **ATFL** first, then the CFL, from inversion with plantarflexion. Anterior drawer and talar tilt tests assess these ligaments.

**Common fibular nerve injury** at the fibular neck, from fracture, a tight cast, prolonged leg crossing or knee dislocation, causes **foot drop** with a high-stepping gait, weak eversion and numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Ankle inversion and the ankle reflex are preserved, which distinguishes it from an L5 radiculopathy (where inversion is also weak). Nerve conduction studies localise the lesion.

Surgically, the free fibula flap is a mainstay of head-and-neck and limb reconstruction.

keyPoints: Thin lateral bone of the leg; carries little weight
Lateral malleolus forms the outer ankle and reaches lower than the medial
Common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck → foot drop if injured
Weber A/B/C classifies lateral malleolus fractures
Used as a free vascularised bone flap

test.q: Which nerve wraps around the neck of the fibula?
test.explain: Its exposed course against the fibular neck makes it vulnerable to fractures and pressure, causing foot drop.

test.q: A Weber C ankle fracture is located:
test.explain: Weber C is above the syndesmosis, implying syndesmotic injury and usually instability.

test.q: The bump on the outside of the ankle is the ______ malleolus.
test.explain: It belongs to the fibula and extends lower than the medial malleolus.

test.q: Which ligament is usually torn first in a typical inversion ankle sprain?
test.explain: The ATFL is weakest and taut in plantarflexion, so it fails first.

test.q: A high fibular fracture with an ankle syndesmosis injury is a ______ fracture.
test.explain: Always feel the whole fibula in an ankle injury, or this fracture is missed.
